# THE OWNER'S WORDS ON NEURON, BY TOPIC

*2026-10-17*

HOW THIS DOCUMENT WAS MADE (EVERYTHING IN CAPITAL LETTERS IS CLAUDE'S, NOT THE OWNER'S).

THIS IS EVERY MESSAGE THE OWNER WROTE OR SPOKE IN THE NEURON PROJECT THAT WAS SAVED: THE 427 MESSAGES IN THE OWNER_SOURCE FOLDER ON HP (NUMBERED 01 TO 409, 2026-09-30 TO 2026-10-17, PLUS THE MESSAGES SENT TO CODEX) AND THE OWNER'S WORDS FROM THE FIRST DAYS, 2026-09-23 TO 2026-09-30 (126 MESSAGES; 20 FIRST-DAYS MESSAGES THAT ALSO APPEAR IN OWNER_SOURCE ARE SHOWN ONLY ONCE).

NOT ONE OF THE OWNER'S WORDS WAS CHANGED. A PROGRAM CUT EACH MESSAGE INTO PIECES AT PARAGRAPH BREAKS (AND LONG PARAGRAPHS AT THE END OF A SENTENCE), SORTED THE PIECES INTO THE 21 SECTIONS BELOW, AND PRINTED EACH PIECE FROM THE ORIGINAL FILE. EACH PIECE APPEARS EXACTLY ONCE, EITHER IN A SECTION OR IN APPENDIX A. A CHECK AT THE END CONFIRMED THAT EVERY PIECE IS HERE, CHARACTER FOR CHARACTER.

EACH ENTRY STARTS WITH ITS SOURCE IN BRACKETS: [357 · 2026-10-16] IS OWNER MESSAGE 357 OF THAT DAY; [FIRST DAYS · 2026-09-23 10:09] IS A FIRST-DAYS MESSAGE; [TO CODEX · ...] WAS SENT TO CODEX. WHEN THE SAME MESSAGE ALSO HAS PIECES IN OTHER SECTIONS, THE ENTRY SAYS WHICH ONES. [ ... ] MARKS A PLACE WHERE A PIECE OF THE MESSAGE WAS MOVED TO ANOTHER SECTION. INSIDE A SECTION THE ENTRIES ARE IN TIME ORDER.

WHEN THE OWNER PASTED AN AI'S REPORT, A LOG OR A DICTIONARY ENTRY, THAT TEXT IS NOT THE OWNER'S, SO IT WAS MOVED WORD FOR WORD TO APPENDIX A AND A CAPITAL-LETTER NOTE MARKS THE PLACE. WHEN THE OWNER PASTED THEIR OWN DICTATION, IT STAYS IN THE SECTIONS. SEVEN PASTES MIX THE OWNER'S WORDS WITH AI TEXT; THEY STAY IN THE SECTIONS, MARKED AT BOTH ENDS. NOTES THE SAVING SESSIONS HAD WRITTEN INTO THE FILES ARE SHOWN IN CAPITAL LETTERS.

A SECOND CHECK FOUND THAT MANY MESSAGES ALSO HOLD PASTED TEXT WITH NO MARKER: AI REPORTS AND ANSWERS, SPECS AN AI WROTE (FOR EXAMPLE THE "EMBRYONIC MATHEMATICAL CORTEX" BUILD SPEC IN THE FIRST DAYS), LOGS, AND HEADER LINES WRITTEN BY THE SESSIONS THAT SAVED THE FILES. 1,529 PIECES (299,458 CHARACTERS) WERE JUDGED NOT TO BE THE OWNER'S OWN WORDS. THEY WERE MOVED WORD FOR WORD TO APPENDIX A, AND A CAPITAL-LETTER NOTE MARKS EACH PLACE. THE 21 SECTIONS HOLD 1,220 PIECES (770,930 CHARACTERS) OF THE OWNER'S OWN WORDS. WHERE THE CHECK WAS UNSURE IT KEPT THE PIECE AS THE OWNER'S.

THE SORTING INTO SECTIONS AND THE CHECK FOR PASTED TEXT ARE JUDGEMENTS AND CAN BE WRONG; MOVE ANY PIECE WHERE IT BELONGS. THIS COVERS THE MESSAGES UP TO 409 (2026-10-17). NO IDEAS OF CLAUDE'S WERE ADDED.

Because those long ways and shortcuts can change, and whenever they change, everything is back-populated, so that everything that touches that change gets updated to the new location, or the new meaning, or the new whatever, the new memory. That's how the truth shifts, and everything knows how to use the new truth: back-population. That's why learning is slow, but once we've learned it, runtime is fast. So the correct answer is B. But generally it's B, and then when anything changes downstream, or even upstream, back-population solves it.

Now behind the front door, it's supposed to work like this: any time you do a call from the front door that's been called before, that path is already known. So Cortex really doesn't have to do any work on it. Cortex matches up whatever you called directly into the lexicon that already has everything that it needs to know about where to find that data, and you're given that data. If you make a call at the front door that Cortex doesn't know where the data is, there's a separate path that Cortex uses to go and try to find the data. And that new MCP server call is put into—it's populated into the lexicon, such that if that call is ever called again, it knows where to find that data. Now in that path, there is a call from Cortex to one of its workers to make the truth card. And the truth card that you should be handed should give you the—and it might not just be the truth card; 

it might be some other card, another name. But that card that you should be handed should give you the information that Cortex knows to be true at this state, today, right now, or the last time the state was done, right? Such that you know the information that you asked about, if it's there. If it's not there, then Cortex says we don't have information on that, essentially, right? And it also gives you lists of locations, small little chunks that hold the data actually as data, not just some summarized truth card. Such that you could make another call and say, Hey, I need to see the data from locations this, this, this, and this, right? Now this could be a pretty big token dump if you ask for 76 different locations. But each individual location is like 4,000 characters. So cumulatively, you might be able to ask Cortex for a hydration of 100,000 tokens, but it's not 100,000 tokens because you reread 17 or 56 tool calls, and you reread over however many times. 

[ ... ]

So they all can't run off a Wake.md. It has to be Neuron Wake.md or something like that. So it's project-oriented, such that you don't get dumped a 7 million-token file to hydrate. Maybe Wake.md is just the tail, 4,000 chars, of what. So you can still have a 7 million-token file inside Cortex that is basically the build log of what's going on. But when you call it, it's only the last 4,000 characters, or 6,000 characters, or 15,000 characters. It doesn't have to be 4,000 characters, but it should be small. Case in point, here I am 40 minutes into a conversation, voice to text to you, just to try to get you to understand. Now, the key to this system working is those truth cards are not immutable. As the Cortex system changes, those truth cards are automatically updated, such that the first truth card is probably built by an LLM, because we don't know any other way to do it such that you get the information that you need. 

But that specific truth card points to locations that when they change, data is taken out and data is put back in from the new information that exists in Cortex. This might mean that the truth card summary, the truth has changed, such that the new truth is actually this, and the locations have changed because more data on that truth has been accumulated. This is a huge problem, and it starts with the fact that y'all don't understand that you're supposed to use the front door because you have a database key, and it's really fucking easy just to go walk around and grep whatever the hell you want to grep.If you need a tool like grep from the front door, then build it. The only downside is, is that tool is supposed to be such that it only returns you the locations of the data that's in the grep. So inside the database, you might grep the word Cortex, and it might return you 4,000 locations in your grep, right? 

And maybe each one of those locations—that's probably too many. Let's say it returns you, you know, something that says there's 4,000 instances of Cortex in the Cortex database. Your grep is too broad. You need to say grep Cortex and then a topic, or something like that. But once the grep is done correctly through the front door, then Cortex can say grep Blink has 674 locations. This is the list of the locations, and a small summary of, like, one sentence of what each location is about. And maybe even the size: 4,000 characters, 7,000 characters, 2,000 characters, 15 characters, such that then you can grep each one of those locations to hydrate what you need to hydrate. Not all of the locations. You can look at it and say, Oh, well, I need grep Cortex Blink location 724C7, which is 5,600 characters of what Blink is, per the owner. The grep, the actual freaking grep, would be run by the Cortex, who doesn't give a shit about tokens. 

Cortex itself doesn't care. It's a runtime, generally. It can run billions of tokens in there and not cost us anything but a little bit of electricity. But you cost per token used, per token outputted, and per token reread. So every token you see, every token you work over, and every token you output actually costs me money. But fuck, Cortex can run 75 million tokens on a turn internally, and it doesn't cost me anything. The trick is: how do we figure out how to balance running through the front door such that you choose to use the front door only when you're not building the actual system behind the front door? And the system behind the front door can run all those fucking tokens it wants to run, and it doesn't cost us a damn thing as long as it's not running them through a frontier LLM. 

The worst case would be that we use the front door such to run a frontier LLM that are attached to Cortex behind the front door, so that you end up running 50 million tokens through a different LLM on your turn. That would be bad. That would be contrary to what the whole system is supposed to do.But the yin and yang of it is that if you make a tool call through the MCP that has never been asked before, then Cortex might have to run an LLM back there and have them parse over a hundred thousand tokens to build that truth card and build that tool call, such that it can return to you the information that you need to not burn your tokens endlessly. As that lexicon tool call database gets built out to 50,000, 100,000, 500,000 different tool calls, then all of a sudden it doesn't have to go to an LLM to build the tool call path to get that data ever again. 

It only has to do it one time, and then that tool call path Cortex knows what it's supposed to do to satisfy that tool call path. And that tool call path self-populates as the data changes. Such that if I say grep Cortex blink owner, owner statuses, or owner description. If since the last time you did that, the owner has put in new data that changes the way that that truth card should look in the Cortex, the truth card for that grep would be different. It would have different locations or added locations. It would have maybe a different summary that was an added summary, not because an LLM put it in there, because Cortex put it in there. Because Cortex knows how to disseminate and read over its data and reason over it and all those other things. EVERYTHING IN THIS APPENDIX IS TEXT THAT CAME INSIDE THE OWNER'S MESSAGES BUT IS NOT THE OWNER'S OWN WORDS: PASTES OF AI TEXT, LOGS AND DICTIONARY ENTRIES (A01 TO A33 WERE MARKED AS PASTES IN THE FILES; THE REST WERE FOUND BY THE SECOND CHECK). IT IS NOT CLAUDE'S EITHER. IT IS KEPT WORD FOR WORD.

```
es—there are parts worth salvaging. Do not delete V16 or start another blind rebuild. The expression storage and stored-destination traversal work in the tested cases; the memory, arrival-context, and correction mechanisms need repair or replacement.   NEURON_V16_INDEPENDENT_AUDIT
1. Why five databases?
They are five separate experiment brains—not five components required to run Cortex. Each database contains its own gates, DNA, forms, events, runs, and memories.   NEURON_V16_INDEPENDENT_AUDIT
The uploaded snapshot came from /home/exnulla/neuron-v16. Its databases are:
/home/exnulla/neuron-v16/runs/
├── 20260929_174509/
│   ├── cortex.db     Original trained experiment
│   ├── control.db    Experiment with a key teaching example withheld
│   └── twin.db       Independent repeat to check reproducibility
└── 20260929_183801-groups/
    ├── grow.db       Connected growth from fast = X
    └── islands.db    Expanded mapping containing all 44 islands

All 44 islands are inside one islands.db. There is no database per island. We should leave these experiment records untouched.
2. Which Python files actually matter?
First enter your working directory:
cd /home/exnulla/neuron-v16

These are the six core files. Their line numbers refer to the uploaded version; your live files could have changed.
File    What its code actually does
substrate.py    Defines the database tables and functions to store/read gates, DNA, forms, runs, and memories. Schema: lines 15–43.
encoder.py    Splits incoming text into forms, records metadata, looks up their gates, and decodes output. Timestamp: line 24.
walk.py    Traverses the remaining input. Reads a matching DNA destination or jumps to the next input gate. Main loop: lines 13–35.
query.py    Coordinates an input: encode → walk → record steps → remember → decode. ask(): lines 46–66.
canon.py    Uses SymPy during learning to normalize expressions, substitute into formulas, and find inverses.
learn.py    Chooses candidate formulas, places words, creates relationship DNA, and back-populates. learn(): line 158 onward.


Those six files total 763 lines, including comments and blank lines—not thousands.   NEURON_V16_INDEPENDENT_AUDIT
The other main files are supporting material:
experiment.py                 Runs the original experiment/control/twin
grow.py                       Runs the connected-growth/islands comparison
test_v16.py                   Tests
teacher/formulas.json         Candidate formula library
teacher/curriculum.json       Original lessons
teacher/groups_2026-09-29.json Expanded word-group lessons
runs/.../source/               Preserved code copies from each experiment

The copies under runs/.../source/ are historical evidence—not additional runtime components.
To inspect any working file:
cat walk.py                  # Print it
less -N walk.py               # Read with line numbers; q exits
nano walk.py                  # Open for editing

3. Where the “brain” actually lives
The learned state is in SQLite, not separate Python files for every neuron. The schema defines these eight tables:   NEURON_V16_SOURCE_EVIDENCE
Table    Contents
gate    One expression location, such as X or 1/X.
form    External form ↔ gate mappings.
dna    Gate-selection keys and stored destinations, or answer-template references.
receipt    Answer templates—despite the misleading name.
event    Original input and metadata, including its timestamp.
run    One execution’s input, output, and outcome.
run_step    Its recorded traversal steps.
memory    A reference to a run and its originating event.


For example, the entire current memory structure is:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS memory(
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  event_id INTEGER NOT NULL
);

That is a reference record, not yet your memory neuron with its own mathematical address and DNA.
4. What happens when you enter something?
For a recognized input, query.py currently does:
encoder.encode()       Record input event; resolve forms to gates
sub.add_run()          Create run record
walk.walk()            Traverse stored destinations
sub.add_step()         Save the resulting steps
sub.end_run()          Save output and outcome
sub.remember()         Insert memory reference
sub.commit()           Commit database changes
encoder.decode()       Render output gates as text

The code implementing that sequence is query.py, lines 46–66. Therefore, running query.py is not read-only: even asking a question changes the selected database.   NEURON_V16_SOURCE_EVIDENCE
5. Timeline, space, structure—from the beginning
That gives us a useful order for examining the foundation: time and event identity, expression locations, then the structure connecting them. It does not require throwing away the existing evidence.
There is already a starting point for back-populating chronology:
memory.event_id → event.meta["when"]
memory.run_id  → run → run_step

The timestamp is supplied here, in encoder.py:24:
meta["when"] = meta["when"] or time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z")


It is currently text metadata, not learned mathematical timeline structure.   NEURON_V16_SOURCE_EVIDENCE
My recommendation: preserve those records and use their recorded times when establishing timeline connections. That can give existing memories a chronological access path without copying their contents. It cannot recover events that were never recorded, or invent missing event boundaries.
For the next organism, your requirement is stronger: every recorded occurrence—learning, work, failure, correction, anything—must be chronologically reachable from its beginning. Not just successful question runs, which is what the current memory-publication path largely covers.   NEURON_V16_INDEPENDENT_AUDIT
First action: inspect the existing foundation, without executing it.
cd /home/exnulla/neuron-v16
nl -ba substrate.py | sed -n '15,43p'

That shows the complete table structure. Start there; no edits yet.

V16.1 — structural instructions for Claude
1. Preserve V16; build the corrected structure separately.
   Inspect /home/exnulla/neuron-v16 first. Keep its databases and source as evidence. Start the new organism from zero, recording its creation and subsequent changes from the beginning. Do not preload the vocabulary to hide missing developmental steps.
2. Make definitions graph-readable memory.
   Each definition attaches to its parent gate and contains ordered expression data, context, provenance, and revision history—not merely a run reference. “Definition,” “verb,” “noun,” and other indicators must themselves resolve to graph expressions, not hidden Python flags. Unknown definitions stay unknown. Keep separate sense/context branches within the definition: the feather meaning in your down example must not inherit spatial-direction rules.
3. Build reverse paths when definitions are written.
   Maintain:
   referenced expression
       → definition occurrences containing it
           → owning gates
   
   These are rebuildable access paths into the actual definitions—not another authoritative classification system. Match exact expression references and structural roles, not text substrings. Distinguish “contains this expression” from “asserts this grammatical class”; support explicit AND/OR conditions. A definition mentioning verbs must not automatically classify its owner as a verb.
4. Replace global back-population with targeted, incremental work.
   Each learned formula carries an expression-based applicability selector. Formula changes select matching definition branches; definition changes reconsider the formulas that depend on those changed indicators. Include unnamed gates when they qualify. Matching selects candidates; mathematical fit and applicable evidence determine acceptance.
   Process bounded, resumable batches; deduplicate by formula revision, target, and definition revision. Never retire unrelated DNA. V16 currently retires live shards absent from its rebuilt global set, so merely restricting its loop would damage unrelated structure.   NEURON_V16_SOURCE_EVIDENCE
5. Establish clock input and timeline access at genesis.
   A physical clock may supply a time observation; teach its expression representation and calendar relationships through the boundary. Preserve observed time and recording order separately. Timeline entries reference specific memory occurrences, not copied memory contents. Support seeking a time interval and walking forward/backward; event-continuation links handle activities spanning days. Do not require walking from creation to find Friday.
6. Implement the complete memory/output continuation.
   work remainder exhausted
   → identify/create route-memory neuron
   → append this occurrence with exact route and DNA revisions
   → attach its time reference
   → publish output to the decoder mailbox
   
   Repeating a route means another occurrence—not another copy of its structure. Commit memory and timeline linkage consistently; retries must not duplicate occurrences. Keep definition-memory content distinct from execution receipts. Internal back-population instructions remain expression runs—no decode-to-English/re-encode loop.
7. Add graph-owned relocation and correction.
   A better placement first becomes a supported proposal. On acceptance, transfer the current definition associations, applicable DNA, and encoder/decoder mapping to the new expression location; reconsider only affected dependencies. This is more than changing a word label.
   Do not rename the old canonical expression or rewrite historical receipts. Preserve the prior placement and exact revisions used by old runs. An occupied destination requires explicit conflict resolution; an approved two-node swap must publish atomically. Every correction is itself recorded on the timeline.
8. Prove the structure before expanding vocabulary.
   Demonstrate: marker selection finds matching named and unnamed gates; unrelated gates remain untouched; revising one definition triggers only affected work; repeated runs produce distinct timed occurrences; relocation preserves historical recall; restart resumes incomplete work safely. Instrument inspected rows/gates as unrelated data grows—do not claim 50-billion-neuron scalability from a tiny test.
Host boundary: storage, exact matching, transactions, clock input, and generic traversal may be substrate machinery. Applicability, definitions, and operation sequences must be inspectable graph content. Any temporary Python behavior substituting for an unfinished graph run must be identified explicitly—not reported as a learned capability.

### PASTE A03 · IN MESSAGE 06 · 2026-09-30

```
**The largest omissions are uncertainty, downstream correction, richer language mappings, and reusable runs.** Your brief covers much of the storage repair, but these determine whether the structure can learn, admit what it lacks, and revise its understanding.

I reviewed V16’s source and tests against the earlier versions’ designs, owner statements, and selected implementations. V13’s directory is empty. I left the active V16.1 build alone, ran no experiments, and made no writes—including Cortex records. These are gaps in **V16 and the brief**, not claims about what the builder has implemented meanwhile.

I would add the following.

1. **An incomplete run must remain an explicit unresolved need.**

   V16 reports unknown words, but when it knows the words and lacks a connecting shard, it jumps directly to the next input gate. Without an answer receipt, it returns the route. That permits traversal completion without establishing an answer. V16 traversal (neuron-v16/walk.py:13)

   Preserve the stopping point, unresolved remainder, context, and missing dependency. A later relevant lesson should reactivate that need without requiring the question again. Earlier V11 recorded this behavior for unanswered questions. Distinguish **answered, echoed, unknown, ambiguous, contradicted, and interrupted** through graph expressions. An explicitly learned jump can remain valid; a missing relationship must not silently become one. V11 results (neuron-v11/RESULTS\_2026-09-25.md:40)
2. **Retain competing explanations and their evidence.**

   Your brief says evidence determines acceptance, but does not specify what survives when several formulas fit—or none does. V16 chooses the first compatible assignment from its candidate ordering. It also reports the same failure when its search cap is reached and when no assignment is found. Formula selection (neuron-v16/learn.py:126)

   Keep candidates, assumptions, supporting observations, counterexamples, and reasons for rejection. Separate mathematical derivation from the hypothesis that a formula represents a linguistic relationship. Repeated traversal increases familiarity; it supplies no new independent observation by itself. V15 had an explicit test for that distinction. The acceptance and evidence-combination rules should themselves be inspectable, revisable graph content. Familiarity test (neuron-v15/tests/test\_v15.py:244)
3. **Correction must invalidate dependent conclusions, not just relocate a gate.**

   Reverse definition links answer “where does this expression occur?” They do not completely answer “which conclusions relied on this particular assertion or DNA revision?”

   Preserve dependency links from evidence and formula revisions through derived shards, answer routes, and current interpretations. When support is withdrawn, reconsider those dependents—including cached answers. If another independent justification remains, preserve it.

   V15 already maintained dependent-shard invalidation and traced affected memories back to the wrong hop. Carry that requirement forward through graph operations rather than copying its Python implementation. Invalidation (neuron-v15/neuron15/computer.py:1767), correction tracing (neuron-v15/neuron15/computer.py:2926)
4. **Sense branches need a matching encoder/decoder model.**

   Definition branches alone cannot fix V16’s boundary: it resolves each word to one current gate and explicitly tests that two words never share a gate. Form lookup (neuron-v16/substrate.py:94), uniqueness test (neuron-v16/test\_v16.py:76)

   Allow a form to resolve to different expressions according to language and context, and allow different forms to express the same established meaning. Some boundary mappings may produce an ordered expression sequence, as in your `caminar` example.

   Likewise, do not assume every relation has exactly one valid answer. Multiple answers may represent legitimate alternatives, missing context, ambiguity, or disagreement. Your adopted Q22 material explicitly distinguishes these. Avoid automatically merging meanings or splitting them merely because a contradiction appeared. Owner/Q22 record (neuron-v15/spec/OWNER\_ANSWERS\_Q21\_Q22\_2026-09-29.md:15)
5. **A stored run must be usable as a component of another run.**

   Appending a receipt is insufficient for your “runs on top of runs” idea. The graph needs to represent entry, argument bindings, continuation, result, and where execution resumes after a subrun. When two results are needed, their dependency and joining point must also be represented.

   V16 only walks a flat input list. Earlier V15 stored execution order and dependencies in plan DNA, with tests for independent branches joining. That supplies useful historical evidence for the requirement, without making its particular plan representation mandatory. V16 loop (neuron-v16/walk.py:16), V15 dependency tests (neuron-v15/tests/test\_v15.py:322)

   **Acceptance example:** a learned inner run is reused inside a new outer run; its receipt identifies the actual inner execution and the outer continuation.

### PASTE A04 · IN MESSAGE 07 · 2026-09-30

```
6. **Preserve mathematical domains and the expression that produced an address.**

   “Canonical expression” needs a precise contract. V16 uses `factor(cancel(e))`; its gate stores the resulting expression. The brief should explicitly retain the original expression, substitution bindings, assumptions, and canonicalization version behind that result. Canonicalization (neuron-v16/canon.py:19)

   For example, cancelling X/X requires retaining the exclusion of X=0; an inverse can require a domain or branch choice. Otherwise normalization can erase information needed to determine applicability.

   Mathematical equivalence, sharing a location, and semantic equivalence must remain distinguishable. A coincident address is evidence to investigate, not sufficient proof that two meanings are interchangeable.
7. **Historical recall and present reinterpretation need separate operations.**

   Your timeline records when things happened, but the system must distinguish:
   - What was observed?
   - What did it conclude then?
   - What does it conclude now about that observation?

   V16’s replay runs the old input through current DNA, then decodes both the old and new outputs using current word mappings. Consequently, its displayed “then” is not a faithful historical rendering after mappings change. Replay (neuron-v16/query.py:69)

   Preserve the original observation and interpretation revisions. Historical reconstruction should use the applicable old mappings; reinterpretation should create a new linked interpretation. Your turtle/tortoise example was already represented by a V15 test that required the observation to remain unchanged. Reinterpretation test (neuron-v15/tests/test\_v15.py:150)
8. **Bounded batches do not prevent unbounded generation.**

   Applying formulas to newly created unnamed gates can produce endless families—for example, repeated cubing yields X³, X⁹, X²⁷,…. Small batches merely spread that work over time.

   Specify what justifies materializing another gate, which unfinished dependencies deserve work, and how duplicate or cyclic derivations are recognized. Distinguish a genuine stopping point from a laboratory pause or exhausted budget. Pending old work must not indefinitely starve new observations.

   This is a demonstrated historical problem: V12 recorded runaway work on inappropriate domains and retry queues starving new conjectures. V12 findings (neuron-v12/OPEN\_QUESTIONS.md:64)
9. **The teaching/correction loop needs an explicit target and observable outcome.**

   Preserve a feedback event’s link to the exact occurrence, proposed answer, or decision being corrected. Praise, refusal, a factual correction, and a reported consequence are different observations. A delayed “no” must not accidentally correct whichever answer happened most recently.

   The graph should also be able to expose an unresolved question and receive its answer through the boundary. Your earlier requirements included learning from consequences and asking the source likely to know—not merely receiving a stream of relation triples. Owner’s feedback and consequence discussion (neuron-v15/spec/OWNER\_ANSWERS\_Q14\_Q18\_2026-09-29.md:7)

   A full feeling or consequence model can come later. **The occurrence links and feedback path should exist now.**
10. **Verify faithful execution, not only correct-looking output.**

    Add structural checks alongside your existing acceptance list:
    - Each recorded hop uses a shard belonging to its actual source gate.
    - Every branch waits for the dependencies recorded in the graph.
    - A run crossing a correction uses a defined, coherent revision policy.
    - Repeated known runs reuse learned structure without silently rebuilding it.
    - Timing includes encoding, lookup, receipt persistence, timeline attachment, and output delivery—not just the inner hop loop.

    Earlier V15’s audit found receipts claiming hops from a gate that did not own the shard. V16’s reported `walk_microseconds` excludes recording and decoding. These matter directly to the claims about faithful traversal and cheap use. Historical receipt failure (neuron-v15/spec/V15\_V151\_FORENSIC\_AUDIT\_NOTES.md:65), V16 timing boundary (neuron-v16/query.py:56)

I would also preserve **later work items** for self-proposed relationships, analogy across domains, learned evidence reliability, memory salience, and specialist brains. Earlier versions explored parts of these, but they should not all become V16.1 prerequisites. The immediate priority is retaining the evidence, dependencies, ambiguity, and executable continuations those capabilities will need.

I checked the current formula generator (neuron-v16.2/canon.py:47). It varies integer parameters, composes pairs from the existing library, removes equivalent expressions, and orders candidates by complexity. It is deterministic, rather than random, but your larger point holds: **it explores a relatively narrow family of algebraic expressions.** I did not independently verify the count of approximately 240.

Below are **73 candidate families**, with representative mathematics, possible Neuron uses, and sources. This is a research catalog, not a recommendation to install everything. The mathematics comes from the cited work; **the proposed Neuron applications are my suggestions**, unless stated otherwise. Some entries are mathematical systems or algorithms rather than single equations.

One distinction matters throughout: a formula for **where a meaning belongs**, a formula for **executing an operation**, and a formula for **assessing evidence** have different jobs. They can all live as graph content without being interchangeable.

**For mathematical locations and relationships**, I would explore these families first.

| \# | Family and representative form | Possible use in Neuron | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Affine transformations:** f(x)=Mx+b | Relationships involving several dimensions at once. Translation, scaling, reflection, and rotation become special cases. | [MIT: linear algebra, least squares, and SVD (https://www.ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-34-numerical-methods-applied-to-chemical-engineering-fall-2015/b3d5967d107c09284ab273a74fa33212\_MIT10\_34F15\_Lec06.pdf)](<https://www.ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-34-numerical-methods-applied-to-chemical-engineering-fall-2015/b3d5967d107c09284ab273a74fa33212_MIT10_34F15_Lec06.pdf>) |
| 2 | **Polynomial and rational families:** f(x)=∑ aₖxᵏ, or P(x)/Q(x) | Broader relationship candidates than fixed multiples and powers. Multivariate versions could depend on context as well as the starting meaning. | [Brunton, Proctor \& Kutz, 2016 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.03580)](<https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.03580>) |
| 3 | **Algebraic laws, inverses, and involutions:** f(f(x))=x, g(f(x))=x | Test the _structure_ of a proposed relationship. A reversible opposition should satisfy different laws from “more,” “part of,” or “causes.” | [Knuth \& Bendix, 1970 (https://www.cs.tufts.edu/\~nr/cs257/archive/don-knuth/knuth-bendix.pdf)](<https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/don-knuth/knuth-bendix.pdf>) |

Your puzzle idea particularly points toward **joint constraint solving**: several relationships constrain the same meaning simultaneously. However, the constraints may determine a structure only up to a translation, rotation, or other symmetry. A unique numerical address additionally needs reference points or a canonical convention. Also, conflicting constraints can reveal a mistaken observation, an inadequate formula family, or two senses that were incorrectly merged.

**My recommendation is to prioritize the mathematics that lets Neuron discover, explain, and correct its own structure.** For your present stage, I would put these first:

1. **Unification, anti-unification, and graph rewriting**—match expressions, extract shared patterns, and execute learned transformations.
2. **Joint constraints and counterexample-guided synthesis**—revise formulas and placements together instead of finding one convenient pairwise fit.
3. **Minimum description length plus unseen examples**—distinguish reusable relationships from elaborate memorization.
4. **Provenance and truth maintenance**—know why a placement or conclusion exists and what must change when its support fails.
5. **Four-valued standing plus calibrated uncertainty**—preserve unknowns and contradictions as actionable states.
6. **Value of information and bounded exploration**—choose useful internal work without unrestricted fan-out.
7. **Contracts and temporal logic**—connect actual behavior to the owner’s scope.

For example, when `big → huge` suggests 3A, the next useful step is not automatically trying every larger power. Neuron could identify another relationship that constrains both meanings, find where competing candidates disagree, request or retrieve that discriminating example, and revise the affected structure. If several formulas still fit, it should retain that uncertainty and the next useful question.

Each candidate also needs its **domain, applicable context, evidence, counterexamples, dependencies, revision, and execution cost** represented alongside it. Otherwise a richer library simply makes it easier to find an impressive-looking equation that fits yesterday’s examples.

The forward run can remain short where learning has already resolved the work. But arbitrary new inputs still require real matching, substitution, traversal, and sometimes calculation; these papers do not justify a universal “nearly zero compute” claim.

Yes. I found published mathematics for the separate operations you’re describing—and systems that explicitly combine several of them. The closest matches to your unknown-node example are constraint propagation, abductive interpretation, structural analogy, and non-axiomatic reasoning. Computer Science at UBC
These are mathematical ingredients to investigate, not proposed replacements for Cortex. I’ve normalized the notation; formulas marked schematic summarize a method rather than quote one equation. The papers’ variables describe premises and structures—not assignments to Cortex gates.
Finding what an unknown node could mean
1. Substitution and unification — Robinson; Hart, MIT, 1965
\[
\theta=\operatorname{mgu}(s,t),
\qquad s\theta=t\theta
\]Find the most general substitution that makes two structured expressions agree. For your example, matching a relationship with a missing destination against an existing relationship can bind that destination without inventing it.
This supplies structural matching, not a probability or a semantic guess. Source: Timothy Hart, A Useful Algebraic Property of Robinson’s Unification Algorithm. MIT Open Scholarship
2. Constraint propagation — Alan Mackworth, 1977
\[
D_i\leftarrow
\{x\in D_i:\exists y\in D_j,\ C_{ij}(x,y)\}
\]Keep candidate \(x\) only when a compatible candidate remains in the neighboring constraint.
Your application: “opposite of big,” “similar to tiny,” and the definition’s other relationships progressively restrict the unknown’s possible placement. Mackworth also explicitly addresses revisiting affected relationships rather than repeatedly revisiting everything. Local consistency does not guarantee a complete solution. Source: Consistency in Networks of Relations. Computer Science at UBC
3. Abduction: infer the explanation — Hobbs, Stickel, Appelt and Martin, 1993
Schematic optimization:
\[
H^*=\arg\min_H\operatorname{cost}(H)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
B\cup H\models O
\]Here \(B\) is background knowledge, \(O\) the observations, and \(H\) the assumptions explaining them, with consistency required.
Your application: find the interpretation that explains the surrounding relationships with the least unsupported assumption. This is a hypothesis, not a deductively guaranteed fact. Their work applies weighted abduction directly to language interpretation, reference resolution and ambiguity. Source: Interpretation as Abduction. Information Sciences Institute
4. Relational analogy — Dedre Gentner, 1983
Schematic structure-preserving mapping:
\[
R(a,b)\ \mapsto\ R(m(a),m(b))
\]The mapping \(m\) transfers relationships and their organization, not merely similar-looking objects.
Your application: compare big : small with long : short by aligning the relational pattern. This is also relevant to interpreting an “ant beside an elephant” metaphor without claiming an ant literally means “small.” Source: Structure-Mapping: A Theoretical Framework for Analogy. Wiley Online Library
5. Similarity from shared and distinguishing features — Amos Tversky, 1977
\[
S(a,b)=
\theta f(U\cap V)
-\alpha f(U\setminus V)
-\beta f(V\setminus U)
\]\(U,V\) are feature sets; \(f\) measures feature importance.
Compare what two meanings share, while penalizing relevant differences. The weights can reflect the comparison’s context; similarity need not be symmetric.
Your application: compare the unknown’s supported definition features with those of “tiny” and “small.” A high similarity score is not identity, universal interchangeability, or probability of truth. Source: Features of Similarity. UC San Diego Pages
Learning relationships rather than merely storing supplied answers
6. Anti-unification: extract the shared pattern — Plotkin/Reynolds, 1970; Østvold, 2004
An elementary example:
\[
\operatorname{lgg}\bigl(f(a),f(b)\bigr)=f(A)
\]For distinct constants \(a,b\), the least general generalization preserves their common structure while replacing the differing part with a variable.
Your application: discover a reusable expression pattern across examples instead of retaining only each individual example. This does not, by itself, prove the pattern’s semantic applicability. Source: Østvold, A Functional Reconstruction of Anti-Unification, which gives recursive equations and a correctness proof. NR
7. Inductive logic learning — Stephen Muggleton, 1995
A noise-free target specification:
\[
B\cup H\models E^+
\]\[
B\cup H\not\models e^-
\quad\text{for each negative example }e^-
\]Find a hypothesis \(H\) that, with background knowledge \(B\), explains positive examples without also entailing the negative examples.
Your application: infer which relationship rule applies across examples, rather than having the teacher supply every destination. Progol also supports a trade-off between errors and hypothesis complexity. Source: Inverse Entailment and Progol. Imperial College London Documentation
8. Choosing the simplest adequate formula — Jorma Rissanen, 1978
\[
F^*=\arg\min_F\left[L(F)+L(D\mid F)\right]
\]Choose the model with the shortest combined description of the formula and the data remaining unexplained by it.
Your application: evaluate the builder’s claim that Cortex rejected a suggested formula for a simpler, better-fitting one. This is a principled selection criterion—not evidence that the selected formula will generalize until tested. Here “description length” is a modeling criterion, not permission to delete original evidence. Source: Modeling by Shortest Data Description. IBM Research
9. Learn a reusable explanation — Mitchell, Keller and Kedar-Cabelli, 1986
Schematic generalized result:
\[
B\models C(X)\Rightarrow G(X)
\]Explain why one example achieves \(G\), then extract sufficient conditions \(C\) under which the explanation still works.
Your application: retain a reusable reasoning route and its conditions, rather than only the answer reached on one occasion. This is particularly relevant to your distinction between learning the expensive process and reusing established structure. Source: Explanation-Based Generalization: A Unifying View. Springer
Combining evidence and handling uncertainty
10. Bayesian hypothesis comparison — E. T. Jaynes
\[
P(H\mid D)=\frac{P(D\mid H)P(H)}{P(D)}
\]Update the plausibility of an interpretation \(H\) using observed evidence \(D\).
For several evidence items:
\[
P(D_1,\ldots,D_n\mid H)
=
\prod_i P(D_i\mid H,D_1,\ldots,D_{i-1})
\]Important for Cortex: three routes derived from the same source are not automatically three independent observations. The dependence belongs in the model. Source: Probability Theory: The Logic of Science. Bayes' Theorem
11. Multiple weighted logical formulas — Richardson and Domingos, 2006
\[
P(\omega)=
\frac{1}{Z}
\exp\!\left(\sum_i w_i\,n_i(\omega)\right)
\]Here \(\omega\) is a possible interpretation, \(n_i(\omega)\) counts satisfied instances of formula \(i\), and \(w_i\) is its weight.
This directly addresses your “several formulas contributing differently” idea: logical relationships jointly constrain plausible interpretations, rather than each producing an unrelated score.
The weights and probability model need justification. The paper’s particular learning procedure also makes a closed-world assumption; that must not silently become Cortex’s “missing means false” policy. Source: Markov Logic Networks. Homes at UW
12. Deduction, induction, abduction and revision together — Pei Wang, Non-Axiomatic Logic
Using Wang’s inheritance/substitutability relation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S\to M,\ M\to P &\ \vdash\ S\to P
&&\text{deduction}\\
M\to S,\ M\to P &\ \leadsto\ S\to P
&&\text{induction}\\
S\to M,\ P\to M &\ \leadsto\ S\to P
&&\text{abduction}
\end{aligned}
\]I use \(\leadsto\) to emphasize that the latter conclusions are defeasible, not classical logical consequences. Wang additionally defines comparison, analogy, composition, revision, and backward reasoning from questions. This is a particularly close research match to your proposed collection of cooperating reasoning operations. Computer & Info Sciences
Its evidence accounting distinguishes:
\[
f=\frac{w^+}{w^++w^-},
\qquad
c=\frac{w^++w^-}{w^++w^-+k}
\]\(f\) measures positive evidence’s share; \(c\) reflects accumulated evidence relative to a positive parameter \(k\). NARS confidence is not automatically a calibrated probability of being correct. Source: Wang’s author-written account of NARS semantics and rules. Computer & Info Sciences
13. Reasoning without collapsing contradiction into nonsense — Nuel Belnap, 1977
Represent support for a proposition and support against it separately:
\[
(t,f)\in
\{(1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(0,0)\}
\]These distinguish supported only, opposed only, conflicting support, and neither.
Your application: an uncertain or contradictory definition need not become either “false” or an unrestricted source of conclusions. This paper specifically concerns inference-capable question-answering systems with inconsistent databases. Source: A Useful Four-Valued Logic. Springer
14. Track the assumptions behind each conclusion — Johan de Kleer, 1986
A compact description of an assumption label:
\[
L(p)=
\min_{\subseteq}
\{\Delta:
B\cup\Delta\models p,\;
B\cup\Delta\text{ is consistent}\}
\]Store the minimal consistent assumption sets supporting \(p\).
Your application: retain rival interpretations and identify which conclusions depend on an assumption that later fails. This supplies an explicit dependency structure rather than a single confidence number that conceals why something was believed. Source: An Assumption-Based TMS. DOI
Mathematics for language and executable processes
15. Entailment and contradiction through language structure — MacCartney and Manning, 2009
A basic negation relationship:
\[
P\subseteq Q
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\overline Q\subseteq\overline P
\]Negation reverses the direction of inclusion. Their natural-logic framework composes lexical relationships through surrounding linguistic structure.
Your application: a substitution that preserves a claim in one sentence position may reverse or destroy it under “not,” quantifiers, or other contexts. This is especially relevant to Cortex’s contradiction detection. Source: An Extended Model of Natural Logic. ACL Anthology
16. Grammar as algebraic composition — Lambek’s tradition; Coecke, Sadrzadeh and Clark, 2010
A subject–transitive-verb–object type reduction:
\[
n\,(n^{r}s\,n^{l})\,n\ \leq\ s
\]The noun-phrase types cancel the verb’s required argument types, leaving a sentence type.
Your application: ordered parts combine through mathematically specified relationships. Here multiplication means ordered composition, and superscripts indicate adjoints—not ordinary numerical powers. The cited framework also develops meaning composition; adopting its vector representation is a separate choice, not a requirement for Cortex. Source: Mathematical Foundations for a Compositional Distributional Model of Meaning. arXiv
17. Processes themselves expressed algebraically — Dexter Kozen, Kleene Algebra with Tests
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{sequence}(p,q)&=pq\\
\text{if }b\text{ then }p\text{ else }q&=bp+\bar bq\\
\text{while }b\text{ do }p&=(bp)^*\bar b
\end{aligned}
\]These express continuation, conditional choice, and repetition algebraically. Here \(+\) is choice, multiplication is sequence, and \(^*\) is iteration.
Your application: investigate mathematical representations of the runs that select, compare, continue, and terminate—not merely formulas describing word relationships. This algebra specifies behavior; it does not establish zero execution cost. Source: On Hoare Logic and Kleene Algebra with Tests, 2000. Cornell Computer Science
What I would take from this for your experiment
Your unknown-node example need not begin by guessing a word. My proposed sequence is:
match relationships → restrict candidates → compare definition features → form an explanation → check opposing evidence → rank the remaining interpretations.
It could conclude, “This denotes something of small size; ‘tiny’ is a possible substitute in this context,” while still lacking the unknown node’s external name. Inferring a meaning and recovering an unseen spelling are different accomplishments.
Likewise, “formula installed,” “relationship inferred,” and “reasoning process learned” are different claims. Selecting a formula from an existing library can be genuine inductive learning when it generalizes; it does not prove that the selection or reasoning happens inside the graph. The inference methods above provide ways to test that distinction. Imperial College London Documentation
And “98%” needs more than a convincing trace or a normalized score. Require the probability model, the evidence it used, and performance on withheld cases. Predictions near 98% should succeed at approximately that rate over a sufficiently large, relevant test population. Calibration is a separate measurable property—not something obtained by naming a field confidence.

### PASTE A13 · IN MESSAGE 56 · 2026-10-01

cool·ness /ˈkuːlnəs/ noun

The state or quality of being moderately cold; a pleasant lack of heat. "the coolness of the evening air"
Calm self-possession; freedom from agitation, especially under pressure. "he handled the crisis with remarkable coolness"
A lack of friendliness, warmth, or enthusiasm; reserve. "there was a noticeable coolness between the two families"
(informal) A quality of effortless, self-assured style that others find admirable or desirable. It is marked by authenticity, composure, and a perceived independence from the need for approval. "his coolness came from not caring whether anyone was watching"
(of color) The quality of a hue tending toward blue, green, or violet. "the coolness of the gray-blue palette"

Origin: Old English cōlnes, from cōl ("cool") + -nes ("-ness"). Sense 4 developed from 20th-century African American jazz culture of the 1930s and '40s, where "cool" described a relaxed, controlled, understated style of performance and bearing.

Synonyms: composure, poise, aplomb, sangfroid (sense 2); aloofness, reserve, distance (sense 3); style, charisma, swagger (sense 4)

Antonyms: warmth, heat (sense 1); agitation, panic (sense 2); cordiality (sense 3); uncoolness, dorkiness (sense 4)

Usage note: In sense 4, coolness is generally thought to be lost the moment it is pursued. Trying to be cool is widely regarded as its opposite.
```

# Neuron V16.2 — focused independent audit, 2026-10-01

## Scope and verdict

The owner's question is whether learning, encoding, and execution policies still live in host Python, whether a reported approximately 15-minute sweep revisits the corpus, and whether graph-owned compiler work is genuine. This review audits those boundaries, not all possible architectural invariants or unseen live changes.

**Verdict:** there is real new graph-owned execution and cached-result reuse. Learning strategy and meaning selection remain substantially Python-owned. A synchronous revision search blocks the organism's single event loop. The approximately 15-minute periodic whole-corpus sweep is **not established** by this archive. Other broad passes do exist, with different triggers and scopes.

No owner runtime, service, source, or original database was changed. Executions used copied source, disposable databases, or a scratch copy of the living database. SQL inventory queries were audit operations, not organism workloads.

## 1. Evidence and collection limits

- Input: `neuron-audit-20261001T081814Z-p8069ckc-PARTIAL.tar.gz`.
- Archive SHA-256: `dbc83e767515f03035f64c7ff1e2361aa1ef79ace414556800d06fa5ece314c3`, matching the supplied companion checksum.
- All **1,237 manifest-listed files** verified; no missing entries or mismatches. The checksum manifest itself is not self-listed.
- The archive contains **106 SQLite snapshots**, mostly historical experiments and benchmarks. This audit opened the V16.2 living snapshot and ran its SQLite `quick_check`, which returned `ok`. It did not independently integrity-check all 106 databases.
- Living snapshot: **40,331 gates**, **330,229 DNA rows**, **14,012 events**, **6,394 work records**. Work state: **6,390 done, 4 paused, 0 open**. Inbox: **4,124 done, 1 rejected, 0 open**. These are snapshot counts, not a throughput proof or a statement that every concept is correct.
- `PARTIAL` reflects **44 withheld credential-pattern-containing files**, all under the older `cortex-substrate` source tree, and **three changed transcript-sweep state/lock files** there. The collector reports no errors or warnings and no detected changes to captured V16.2 source. This does not make the multi-file collection atomic.
- The older substrate's `scripts/transcript_sweep.py` is among the withheld files. Installed/running services, process profiles, remote corpus databases, and the externally referenced `/home/exnulla/neuron-benchmarks/` reports were not captured. I do not infer their live contents.

All code references below use `/home/exnulla/neuron-v16.2/` unless otherwise stated. The companion source-evidence document contains exact numbered excerpts and hashes.

## 2. Independent execution

### Supplied tests

**77/77 supplied tests passed unchanged**, using `test_compiler`, `test_graph_owned`, `test_resume`, and `test_v16_2` in an isolated environment: Python 3.13.5, SymPy 1.14.0, SQLite 3.46.1. Runtime: 46.786 seconds in this container.

An initial run in the default container failed only the no-math-import check because the environment preloads NumPy. A clean virtual environment, using the same installed SymPy/mpmath versions, removed that environmental contamination. It is not counted as a V16.2 defect. Logs for both runs are retained.

These tests cover useful controls: changing graph programs changes writing/clock behavior without a fallback; immutable old code remains; arithmetic works on unseen operands; repeated calculations reuse stored answers; selected operations resume. Passing them is not proof of arbitrary self-improvement, calibrated confidence, or billion-neuron scalability.

### Genuine cached-result reuse

Independent calls of `CALCULATE` on `123 TIMES 17` in a fresh scratch brain:

| Measurement | First call | Repeated call |
|---|---:|---:|
| Output | 2091 | 2091 |
| VM steps | 5,720 | 97 |
| NAND graph entered | yes | no |
| Interrupted | no | no |

No `learn`, `canon`, SymPy, or NumPy module was loaded in this probe. The first call executes the supplied arithmetic graph and stores an answer link; the second reads that link. The initial arithmetic algorithm was **supplied**, not autonomously discovered. The call still performs compilation lookup, validation, record-writing, and traversal work; it is not zero physical work.

Measured durations in the JSON are only these local VM calls. They are **not** whole-inbox/commit/decoder performance measurements and do not support a tokens-per-hour claim.

Sources: `teacher/compiler_runs.json` CALCULATE/CALC_RUN/COMPILER, `instructions.py:80–135`, `calculation_probe.json`.

## 3. Where behavior really lives

| Component | Graph-owned part | Remaining host-owned part |
|---|---|---|
| Writing and clock links | BIRTH, NODELINKS, CLOCKSTEP, CLOCKNOW, OBSERVE, ENTRY and related stored runs select many link operations | `physics._run` selects the overall memory/clock/timeline/mail completion path |
| Compiler | The stored COMPILER program checks a three-item source, selects an operator's implementation link, and assembles a program; CALCULATE chooses cached reuse versus execution | Generic stack/sequence instructions, storage effects, binary representation codecs, execution machinery |
| Back-population | Selectors are persisted; live WORK_PLAN/ADMIT/PREPARE/SAVE programs control some admission, preparation and checkpointing | `learn.py` parses selectors, finds targets, computes symbolic destinations and publishes derived relationships |
| Formula revision | Formula candidates and evidence are persisted | `_suspects`, `_search`, `_positions`, `_apply` decide what to reconsider, what hypotheses to try, and what placements to change |
| Definitions/proposals | Definitions, markers, reverse references and resulting proposals are persisted | `matches`, `consider`, `targets`, `propose` implement substantial selection and inference behavior |
| Encoding | Word/form mappings are persisted | `encoder._resolve` selects a meaning using other words' island roots before the graph run |
| General execution | Stored instruction sequences and learned relation destinations | Python VM dispatch, stack and frames, generic effect implementation, hard resource ceilings |

The current `learn.py` has 1,435 lines, `physics.py` 612, `instructions.py` 145, and `encoder.py` 142, including comments and blanks. These counts describe the files; they are not a measure of cognitive ownership.

**The decisive distinction:** `advance_work` can execute graph WORK_PREPARE, but calls Python `do_work()` for symbolic evaluation/publication afterward (`learn.py:351–429`). A graph-selected quantum does not make the whole learner graph-owned. Likewise, a stored expression named as a procedure is insufficient unless its behavior is actually expressed by its stored run.

Not all Python outside stored nodes is an architectural defect. Generic execution, storage, codecs and hard bounds are distinguishable from choosing meanings, interpreting evidence, accepting a hypothesis, and choosing a learning strategy. Migrating learning means migrating those decisions into versioned graph programs, not storing the text of learn.py in a neuron or adding a special LEARN opcode that invokes the same host function.

## 4. Blocking learning — independently reproduced

The captured builder message `MAILBOX/008_claude_to_codex.md` reports a **29-minute**, unfinished revision on a scratch brain after accepting `happiness opposite sadness`. It explicitly calls its account of the search a source reading, not a profile. I did not rerun it for 29 minutes.

I independently submitted that relation as a lesson to a scratch copy of the captured living database, then queued `quick opposite ?` behind it. A single `Brain.cycle()` was interrupted by the auditor's **20-second external safety deadline**:

- Wall time: **20.000 seconds**; CPU time: **19.974 seconds**.
- `_search`: 1 call, current relation `opposite`.
- `_positions`: **178 calls**.
- `canon.apply`: **13,777 calls**.
- The queued ordinary question remained **open**, with **zero answer mailbox rows**.

This is a synchronous host formula-search blockage, not a demonstrated periodic scan. The search is finite in candidate families, but there is no wall-time budget, resumable candidate cursor, or inbox yield inside this revision path. Existing resumable WORK_PREPARE does not cover it.

**Scope qualification:** `_chain` uses indexed relation and endpoint dependencies. In this snapshot, the opposite placement chain contained **54 placed words**, not the approximately 400 estimated in the builder message. The search repeatedly reevaluates that dependency closure for different formulas. It is not an unconditional scan of all 40,331 neurons or the older multi-million-token corpus. SQLite query plans confirm index use for the chain seed, dependents, and word-connected lines.

Sources: `alive.py:197–216,248–255`; `learn.py:743–788,823–993`; `revision_probe.json`; `query_plans.json`.

## 5. What the sweeps and waits actually are

### No demonstrated 15-minute Neuron timer

The living loop waits on its wake socket and the next clock minute (`alive.py:370–385`). A wake interrupts that wait. No fixed 900-second/15-minute interval appears in the current Neuron loop or learning code inspected.

`talk.Remote.wait` has a **600-second timeout**, not a mandatory ten-minute delay. Lessons normally wait until **all open inbox work, all open background work, and relinking are drained**, not merely until their own event is processed (`talk.py:70–91,139–143`). Thus unrelated pending work from another teacher can extend the wait. The two teachers do not imply two parallel brain executors.

Inside the organism, learning and graph execution are Python function calls in the same process. There is not a separate Python-process/brain-process round trip at every gate. The actual demonstrated stall is the unyielding search, not an established language-boundary wait cost.

### Targeted back-population really improved

`write_def` records reverse references; `consider` reaches selectors through changed markers; `targets` reaches definitions through a selector condition. Names are no longer the only eligibility mechanism for this back-population path. This is materially different from V16's formula-by-every-labelled-gate product.

However, proposal generation still excludes unnamed owners/candidates using `forms_of()` (`learn.py:1110–1145`), and answer teaching enumerates all named stored programs (`learn.py:1371–1386`). The latter query plan includes `SCAN f`. Those remain nonlocal or boundary-dependent behavior, even though they are not whole-corpus semantic sweeps.

### Timeline RELINK is broad, although resumable and graph-owned

Teaching certain structural roles triggers relinking (`learn.py:1266–1267,1328–1329`; the roles are listed in `physics.LINKS`). The stored RELINK_INIT resets its time and entry cursors, then RELINK walks the timeline collections from their beginning in batches of **32 indexed selections**. The live database programs confirm this, not only the fixture. There were **210 relink events** recorded before collection; the request cursor is currently zero/done.

This is an explicit rebuild of chronology links on structural change, not a 15-minute whole-corpus timer. It can still be expensive as history grows. Merely implementing a broad pass inside graph code does not satisfy a requirement for dependency-targeted incremental updates. Its permissible scope should be explicit.

### Older Cortex substrate: incomplete visibility

The captured `cortex-substrate-transcript-sweep.service` describes inotify-selected incremental passes plus a **30-minute full-scan watchdog heartbeat**. That is a service-file description; the actual sweep script was withheld for credential-pattern screening, and installed/running service state is absent. Therefore I cannot establish whether that heartbeat rereads full transcript contents, only checks filesystem state, or is currently active. Do not equate its label with a proven corpus-wide semantic reprocessing cycle.

## 6. Additional cache-correction defect

The positive cached-calculation result needs a correction mechanism.

Independent probe:

1. Calculate `2 PLUS 3`; result **5** is cached on its compiled program.
2. Deliberately revise the existing NAND_0/BIT0 data link via `Substrate.link` (no Python implementation change).
3. CALCULATE returns cached **5**.
4. Directly execute that same compiled instruction sequence against the changed graph: it terminates with **1** in 594 steps.

The changed truth table is an intentional adversarial control, not a claim that ordinary 2+3 equals 1. The finding is that **cached and fresh execution disagree under the same current graph state**. CALCULATE checks for an ANSWER link but does not validate the data dependencies behind that answer. Another tested NAND mutation did not terminate; no partial value from that interrupted test is treated as an answer.

An explicit policy is needed: either results pin immutable dependency revisions, or relevant dependency changes invalidate/rederive the answer. Recording an execution trace alone does not perform invalidation. This matters especially if the brain is to revise its own algorithms.

Sources: `teacher/compiler_runs.json` CALCULATE; `instructions.py:91–100`; `calculation_probe.json`; `cache_variants.json`; independent probe sources.

## 7. Recommended bounded next changes — proposals, not implemented fixes

1. Make formula revision a bounded, resumable job, including candidate and placement progress. Do not hold the entire inbox hostage to `_search`. Pending evidence remains pending, rather than silently lowering standards to finish.
2. Preserve the new selector/reverse-reference mechanism. Make any all-timeline repair explicit; do not reintroduce corpus-wide passes disguised as graph programs.
3. Migrate one actual learning policy at a time: start with existing selector/WORK_PREPARE structure and separate it clearly from the remaining symbolic-evaluation callback. Move formula-choice and revision strategy into inspectable versioned graph programs, with replayable evidence and independent checks. Do not just add a host LEARN engine behind a gate.
4. Move contextual meaning selection out of `_resolve`; the boundary should deliver known mappings and ambiguity, and graph structure should select the applicable meaning. Preserve unknowns rather than inventing placements.
5. Fix learned-result invalidation before relying on cached answers while graph dependencies change. Test learned-process revisions on scratch branches/snapshots before acceptance; preserve prior versions.

**Do not discard the new compiler work.** Controlled graph mutations change its behavior and repeated calculations avoid repeating arithmetic. But those successes do not mean learn.py has moved inside, that the encoder is non-semantic, or that there are no broad passes.

## 8. Reproduction notes

See the evidence ZIP. The source under `worktree/` is the captured V16.2 source and teacher material used by the tests, not edited builder code. Run tests in a clean Python environment with SymPy 1.14.0 and mpmath. The `probes.py calculation` mode uses only temporary databases. The revision probe expects the living snapshot copied to `snapshot/projects/02-neuron-v16.2/home/cortex.db` beneath the evidence root; it makes a second scratch copy before changing anything and applies a 20-second safety deadline. Never point these probes at the owner's live database.

The source archive and its metadata remain the authority for this audit. This report is a derived interpretation and includes explicit measurement and coverage limits.

By word history, NO comes first and NOTHING = no + thing. But "no" is two different words, and that changes your question.

The two "no"s
- The answer "no" ("no, it isn't") comes from Old English nā = ne + ā, "not ever". This one is NOT, the - that flips a pole.
- The amount "no" ("no thing", "no one") comes from Old English nān = ne + ān, "not one". It's the same word as "none". This one means zero.

"Nothing" is built from the amount "no": nān þing, "not one thing". So:
 a thing would be some anti-thing, which has no word. "Nothing" isn't the opposite of a thing; it's zero things. It's the same as the difference between -1 and 0 on your number line.

So NOTHING = 0 * THING. The 31 pieces can't write that, because they have ONE but no zero.

What I'd suggest (my reading, your call):
- ZERO (0) becomes a root piece. It's a location, the origin. That's what your 66th placeholder NOTHING was standing in for [269].
- NOT (-) stays the operator that flips a pole.
- Then:
  - nothing = 0 · thing
  - none = 0 · one
  - no one = 0 · someone
  - never = 0 · time ("not ever")
  - the answer "no" = NOT applied to what was asked

It also lines up your core thurple, "nothing + ??? = somthing" [269]. That becomes 0 + 1 = 1: zero, the unit and the plus. That's the first thing the build does: neuron 0, +1, spawn 1 (steps 6 and 7 of the outline). Meaning and numbers would start from the same place.

So to answer you directly: neither NOTHING nor NO is the root. ZERO is the root, NOT is the operator, and NOTHING is ZERO applied to THING. If you agree, I'll add ZERO to Table 2 and fix the NOTHING row in PRIMES_SORTED.md.
```

### PASTE A28 · IN MESSAGE 339 · 2026-10-15

```
In code and in silicon

for i in range(apples): eat()     # apples = 0 → eat never runs

LOAD r1, [apple_count]   ; r1 = 0000 → the chip sets the zero flag
JZ   done                ; "jump if zero": skip the eating
loop: EAT
      DEC r1             ; one less apple
      JNZ loop           ; go again while not zero
done:

- Zero is a real value in the chip: all bits low, 0000. Loading it sets the zero flag, and the jump skips the work.
- Null has no bit pattern, because 0000 is already zero. So null needs a separate marker next to the value saying "this slot is empty". Databases keep one bit per column for exactly this, and SQLite stores NULL as its own type with no bytes at all. In C, the null pointer is address 0, meaning "points nowhere".

That's the same line you drew with the remainder. Absent (null) means there's nothing to carry, so the run ends where it stands. Zero is a value, and the run carries it on.

Neuron zero's action, as a formula

When heard before a thing, it sets the amount of the next thing to none: zero · X. Anything that later repeats over that amount runs zero times.

Your two "no" nodes take different paths here. "I have no apples" is the amount no, so it's zero · apples, the same as above. "I do not have apples" is the answer no, NOT applied to "have". Both end in the same memory, but by different formulas.
```

### PASTE A32 · IN MESSAGE 355 · 2026-10-16

```
The expression bloat. Yes, that came from the process, not from your idea. V16 had two causes:
1. The expression was written out every time the gate appeared. Your own rule fixes that: a string is written once, and everything else points to it [107, 311].
2. Runs were stored gate by gate. If the next gate is where you stand plus the remainder, a run doesn't need to list its gates. It's the start plus its remainders, which are small numbers. Your 1-to-9 run becomes "start at 1, +1 eight times", and the formula shortcut makes it shorter still. A 60,000-gate run is 60,000 small numbers while it's being learned, and a handful once the shortcut is found.

Your machines. Brains do work this way: regions specialize, densely wired inside and thinly wired between each other. The catch is distance. A hop inside one machine took 5.7 µs in V16. A call from the hub to hp over ssh took 10 to 15 ms when I tried it just now, which is about 2,000 times slower. A link kept open all the time would be faster than that, but still far slower than a hop inside one machine. A run that crossed machines on every step would crawl, so split where the brain hands over whole jobs, not single hops:
- Together, on the fastest machine: the run, active memory, and the sixth. The sixth is the voice inside every run, so it has to sit next to the run.
- Elsewhere: the hc, which does sleep work in batches and sends back the result; long-term memory, which is big and rarely read; and the outside (sources, friends).

Each machine keeps its own storage, and the cores work at the same time. To get there without a redesign later, build the parts as separate files on the hub now; SQLite can hold several open at once. Moving a part later means moving its file and sending it jobs as waiting rows, which is the same call-out you've already seen, just over ssh. Start on one machine, though. Every machine you add is one more thing that can be asleep, unreachable or out of sync, and V16's trouble with copies and lanes was that kind.

What to invent, in this order:
1. The location system: how a meaning becomes a place, so that relationships are arithmetic. Nobody has this. It's yours, and it decides how much has to be stored at all.
2. The engine: a store or kernel spread across your machines and cores, down to the silicon. It comes after the location system, because before then nobody knows the shape of what it has to hold. Building it first would repeat V16's mistake of speeding up the walker while main was down.

SQLite on the hub will carry the location system for a long time: about 2 billion links on the 100 GB you have free.
```

Do not reinterpret this as an LLM memory system, knowledge graph, semantic graph, vector database, neural network, rule engine, expert system, agent framework, or conventional symbolic-AI project.

The organism itself should not need prose labels such as "truth", "unknown", "question", "concept", "love", "dog", "addition", "analogy", "memory", or "reasoning".

Those are descriptions humans may later use to interpret its behavior.»

The immediate goal is to build the smallest substrate capable of being taught its first mathematical structures incrementally, retaining them locally, traversing only the required path, and eventually modifying/growing its own substrate through the same mathematical mechanism by which an external teacher initially modifies it.

A neuron is an addressable mathematical cell.

[

[
i

[
D_i

[

where:

A normal mathematical expression reaches a neuron.
